description: Security Fest talks from Security Fest 2022.

talks.title: Day 1
talks.teaser: Presents day 1 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The recording covers a full conference day made of several separate sessions. It opens with a social engineering talk in which a red teamer describes gaining entry to banks and offices by exploiting staff assumptions about who belongs, using staged roles, props and small USB devices. The speaker argues that awareness training should rely on real cases, follow up with employees after incidents, and treat failed phishing tests as coaching rather than punishment.

The middle sessions turn technical. One speaker shows how to locate publicly exposed webcams and RTSP streams, and describes using them to watch events during the 2022 conflict in Ukraine, along with the practical problems of running and storing many feeds. Another walks through macOS persistence locations beyond launch agents, including shell startup files, PAM modules, periodic scripts and folder actions, and suggests detection ideas for each. A further session demonstrates Electron desktop app flaws, moving from cross-site scripting to code execution through insecure node integration and exposed inter-process communication.

Later talks cover a case where an IoT gateway for a blockchain-rewarded wireless network exposed an unauthenticated scheduler API, leading to root access and a vendor fix. Another session looks at the cyber risks facing satellite ground stations and unencrypted satellite links. The day closes with a talk on writing security blog posts that rank well in search, covering keyword research, domain authority, metadata and link building.

talks.title: Eyes into an active AO during a war
talks.teaser: Discusses eyes into an active AO during a war and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how internet-connected cameras can give an outside observer a live view of the war in Ukraine. It opens with the speaker's history of webcam research, including a 2012 firmware teardown and access-control flaws where a camera's video URL opened without logging in. A one-line shell pipeline combining Shodan results, a port check and curl requests shows how old-school scripting can test a known weakness across many hosts. Recorder options, from cheap hardware to the open-source Shinobi software, round out the opening.

The core covers wartime work. Scanning Ukrainian address space found several hundred thousand live hosts, about 47,000 RTSP responders, and roughly 2,500 streams with no password. Rooftop cameras with microphones picked up live news reporting, one feed replayed looped footage, and others showed police stations, shelling and defaced cameras. Feeds dropped as power and internet failed. The speaker also describes a web SDR for listening to Russian radio and geolocating cameras with IP lookups and shadows.

The closing section covers practical limits such as ffmpeg zombie processes, heavy CPU use and unstable routing. He argues that red teams holding camera credentials can export RTSP streams without disrupting operations, and blue teams can correlate footage with badge logs. He concludes that many real problems come from unknown perimeter assets rather than exotic attacks.

talks.title: How to write a BANGER blogpost! (Hacking the Google algorithm)
talks.teaser: Explores how to write a BANGER blogpost! (Hacking the Google algorithm) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security researchers should publish their work where people can find it, and that a personal domain and brand outlast job changes that come every few years. It covers the basics of search engine optimisation: keyword research using search volume and difficulty figures, choosing a domain and whether a country-specific top-level domain helps, and registering a site with Google Search Console so its pages get indexed. Domain authority is explained as something built from backlinks, with nofollow links offering a way to avoid passing credit to a competitor.

The middle of the talk works through examples. A competitor analysis compares word counts, keyword density and image filenames, and suggests longer articles with descriptive filenames, alt text and an embedded video, since search engines also surface video results. Titles and meta descriptions should read clearly in search results, and social sharing tags control how links look on social networks. Cached link previews can be refreshed with the platform's validator. For tracking, a short redirect on a personal domain can replace long campaign URLs. A write-up on an NTLM relay technique, with step-by-step instructions, copyable commands and a short video, is presented as a case that reached the top result.

The closing takeaway is to provide real value, avoid keyword stuffing and black-hat tactics, proofread the post, and treat each article as a long-lived asset that keeps driving traffic after the author moves on.

talks.title: Hacking Network APIs
talks.teaser: Examines hacking Network APIs and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, the creator of Packet Sender demonstrates practical techniques for reverse engineering network APIs, analyzing simulated malware traffic, and diagnosing network degradation. Using Packet Sender alongside Wireshark and hardware such as a Raspberry Pi 400 and a KMAX network emulator, the speaker walks through live demonstrations illustrating how devices communicate over raw TCP and UDP sockets, how to mimic or spoof network services, and the crucial distinction between network latency and throughput.

### Key Topics
- **Packet Sender Capabilities**: An overview of the open-source tool Packet Sender, covering GUI and CLI usage, support for TCP, UDP, SSL/TLS, custom delimiters, persistent connections, packet resending, built-in macro strings, smart responses, and UI panel generation.
- **Protocol Reverse Engineering**: Analyzing custom IoT protocols by inspecting Wireshark traffic and using Packet Sender to capture, replay, and automate control commands.
- **Faking Network Services & Spoofing**: Capturing commands directly by setting Packet Sender to listen on target ports, tricking clients into communicating with a rogue listener, and inspecting simulated outbound malware activity.
- **Latency vs. Throughput**: Demonstrating how network degradation affects application behavior using a KMAX device, and why evaluating both latency and throughput is necessary when troubleshooting.

### Technical Details
- **Reverse Engineering Pi Player**:
  - The speaker uses an open-source demo app called "Pi Player" running on a Raspberry Pi 400. To locate the device, Pi Player sends a UDP broadcast to `255.255.255.255` on port 15000 containing the string `find units`. The Pi responds with `server address: <ip>`.
  - Playback commands (`play`, `next`, `stop`) are transmitted via raw TCP connections to port 15000.
  - The speaker demonstrates two reverse-engineering workflows: capturing packets with Wireshark to recreate commands in Packet Sender, and configuring Packet Sender to listen on port 15000 while responding with its own IP address (`0.99`) to trick the client application into sending its commands directly to Packet Sender.
  - Packet Sender's panel generator is used to create a custom graphical dashboard to trigger commands and script sequences (such as `play`, delay 5 seconds, and `stop`).
- **Simulated Malware Analysis**:
  - In an isolated network, an IoT device attempts an ARP request for default gateway `192.168.0.1` to access the Internet.
  - The host adds an alias IP address for the gateway to observe further traffic. The malware attempts a connection to external IP `138.197.192.84` on port 5123.
  - The host configures that external IP as another alias address and runs a persistent TCP listener in Packet Sender on port 5123. The captured payload reveals an Nmap scan report containing OS details, host scanning results, and open ports, representing an exfiltration attempt to a command-and-control server.
- **Latency vs. Throughput Demonstration**:
  - Using Python HTTP servers on ports 8000 and 8001 and VLC RTP media streaming on ports 5004 and 5005, network traffic is selectively degraded using a KMAX hardware emulator.
  - **Rate Limiting (Low Throughput, Low Latency)**: Port 8001 traffic is throttled to 100 kbps while ping latency stays sub-millisecond, causing identical file transfers to take days on one port while completing rapidly on an unshaped port.
  - **Delay Insertion (High Latency, High Throughput)**: A 5-second delay is applied to one of two identical RTP video streams. Both streams sustain identical throughput, but the delay renders synchronous media unusable. The speaker notes human perception detects audio/video discrepancies at 20 to 50 milliseconds.
- **Performance Inefficiency Clarification**: During Q&A, the speaker explains that delays during playback commands occur because Pi Player executes an underlying Linux `system` call to launch an external player and executes a `killall` command to stop playback.

### Takeaways
- Combining a flexible packet generator/listener like Packet Sender with Wireshark enables rapid reverse engineering of proprietary network APIs without needing source code.
- Setting up local listeners and IP aliases allows analysts to safely capture and decode outbound device behavior in isolated sandbox environments.
- Latency and throughput must both be evaluated when assessing network quality; looking at either metric in isolation can completely mask severe performance bottlenecks.
